281-  - Use `have`-expressions to prove the remaining goals
282-  - Use `termination_by` to specify a different well-founded relation
283-  - Use `decreasing_by` to specify your own tactic for discharging this kind of goal
284-n x✝ : Nat
285-h✝ : n.even = true
286-⊢ div2 n < x✝
287--/
288-#guard_msgs in
289-def collatz_holds_for (n : Nat) : Prop :=
290-  match n with
291-  | 0 => False
292-  | 1 => True
293-  | _ => if n.even then collatz_holds_for (div2 n)
294-                   else collatz_holds_for ((3 * n) + 1)
295-
296--- This recursive function is also rejected by the termination
297--- checker, since, while we could in principle convince Lean
298--- that `div2 n` is smaller than `n`, we certainly can't
299--- convince it that `(3 * n) + 1` is smaller than `n`!
300-
301--- Fortunately, there is another way to do it: We can express
302--- the concept "reaches `1` eventually in the Collatz sequence"
303--- as an *inductively defined property* of numbers.
304--- Intuitively, this property is defined by a set of rules:
305-
306---                 ─────────────────── (chf_one)
307---                 CollatzHoldsFor 1
308-
309---   even n = true     CollatzHoldsFor (div2 n)
310---   ─────────────────────────────────────────── (chf_even)
311---                  CollatzHoldsFor n
312-
313---   even n = false    CollatzHoldsFor ((3 * n) + 1)
314---   ─────────────────────────────────────────────── (chf_odd)
315---                  CollatzHoldsFor n
316-
317--- So there are three ways to prove that a number `n`
318--- eventually reaches `1` in the Collatz sequence:
319-
320--- - `n` is `1`;
321--- - `n` is even and `div2 n` eventually reaches `1`;
322--- - `n` is odd and `(3 * n) + 1` eventually reaches `1`.
323-
324--- We can prove that a number reaches `1` by constructing a
325--- (finite) derivation using these rules. For instance, here is
326--- the derivation proving that `12` reaches `1` (where we leave
327--- out the evenness/oddness premises):
328-
329---   ─────────────────────── (chf_one)
330---   CollatzHoldsFor 1
331---   ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
332---   CollatzHoldsFor 2
333---   ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
334---   CollatzHoldsFor 4
335---   ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
336---   CollatzHoldsFor 8
337---   ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
338---   CollatzHoldsFor 16
339---   ─────────────────────── (chf_odd)
340---   CollatzHoldsFor 5
341---   ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
342---   CollatzHoldsFor 10
343---   ─────────────────────── (chf_odd)
344---   CollatzHoldsFor 3
345---   ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
346---   CollatzHoldsFor 6
347---   ─────────────────────── (chf_even)
348---   CollatzHoldsFor 12
349-
350--- Formally in Lean, the `CollatzHoldsFor` property is
351--- *inductively defined*:
352-
353-inductive CollatzHoldsFor : Nat → Prop where
354-  | chf_one  : CollatzHoldsFor 1
355-  | chf_even (n : Nat) : n.even = true →
356-                         CollatzHoldsFor (div2 n) →
357-                         CollatzHoldsFor n
358-  | chf_odd  (n : Nat) : n.even = false →
359-                         CollatzHoldsFor ((3 * n) + 1) →
360-                         CollatzHoldsFor n
361-
362--- For particular numbers, we can now prove that the Collatz
363--- sequence reaches `1` (we'll look more closely at how it
364--- works a bit later in the chapter). Each step applies a rule
365--- and discharges the boolean evenness premise by `rfl`; the
366--- recursive premise is then reduced by the kernel from
367--- `CollatzHoldsFor (div2 12)` to `CollatzHoldsFor 6`, etc.
368-
369-example : CollatzHoldsFor 12 := by
370-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
371-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
372-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_odd;   rfl
373-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
374-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_odd;   rfl
375-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
376-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
377-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
378-  apply CollatzHoldsFor.chf_even;  rfl
379-  exact CollatzHoldsFor.chf_one
380-
381--- The Collatz conjecture then states that the sequence
382--- beginning from *any* positive number reaches `1`:
383-
384-def collatz := ∀ n, n ≠ 0 → CollatzHoldsFor n
385-
386--- If you succeed in proving this conjecture, you've got a
387--- bright future as a number theorist! But don't spend too long
388--- on it -- it's been open since 1937.
389-
390--- Note to developers:
391---     HIDE: CH: We may want to add an exercise later proving
392---     false if one assumes Collatz' conjecture without the
393---     `n ≠ 0` assumption. We had that mistake in the script
394---     for years and no one noticed, wow!
395-
396--- ### Example: Binary relation for comparing numbers
397-
398--- A binary *relation* on a set `α` has Lean type
399--- `α → α → Prop`. This is a family of propositions
400--- parameterized by two elements of `α` -- i.e., a proposition
401--- about pairs of elements of `α`.
402-
403--- For example, one familiar binary relation on `Nat` is
404--- `Le : Nat
405--- → Nat → Prop`, the less-than-or-equal-to relation,
406--- which can be inductively defined by the following two rules:
407-
408---     ─────── (le_refl)
409---     Le n n
410-
411---      Le n m
412---   ───────────── (le_step)
413---   Le n (m + 1)
414-
415-namespace LePlayground
416-
417-inductive Le : Nat → Nat → Prop where
418-  | refl (n : Nat)              : Le n n
419-  | step (n m : Nat) : Le n m → Le n (m + 1)
420-
421-scoped infix:50 (priority := high) " ≤ " => Le
422-
423-example : 3 ≤ 5 := by
424-  apply Le.step; apply Le.step; exact Le.refl 3
425-
426-end LePlayground
427-
428--- ### Example: Transitive Closure
429-
430--- Another example: The *transitive closure* of a relation `R`
431--- is the smallest relation that contains `R` and that is
432--- transitive. This can be defined by the following two rules:
433-
434---                 R x y
435---            ---------------- (t_step)
436---            ClosTrans R x y
437-
438---   ClosTrans R x y    ClosTrans R y z
439---   ------------------------------------ (t_trans)
440---            ClosTrans R x z
441-
442--- In Lean this looks as follows:
443-
444-inductive ClosTrans {α: Type} (R: α→α→Prop) : α → α → Prop where
445-  | t_step (x y : α) :
446-      R x y →
447-      ClosTrans R x y
448-  | t_trans (x y z : α) :
449-      ClosTrans R x y →
450-      ClosTrans R y z →
451-      ClosTrans R x z
452-
453--- For example, suppose we define a "parent of" relation on a
454--- group of people...
455-
456-inductive Person : Type where
457-  | sage
458-  | cleo
459-  | ridley
460-  | moss
461-
462-inductive ParentOf : Person → Person → Prop where
463-  | po_SC : ParentOf .sage .cleo
464-  | po_SR : ParentOf .sage .ridley
465-  | po_CM : ParentOf .cleo .moss
466-
467--- The `parent_of` relation is not transitive, but we can
468--- define an "ancestor of" relation as its transitive closure:
469-
470-def AncestorOf : Person → Person → Prop := ClosTrans ParentOf
471-
472--- Here is a derivation showing that Sage is an ancestor of
473--- Moss:
474-
475---    ———————————————————(po_SC)     ———————————————————(po_CM)
476---    ParentOf .sage .cleo            ParentOf .cleo .moss
477---   —————————————————————(t_step)  —————————————————————(t_step)
478---   AncestorOf .sage .cleo          AncestorOf .cleo .moss
479---   ————————————————————————————————————————————————————(t_trans)
480---                   AncestorOf .sage .moss
481-
482-example : AncestorOf .sage .moss := by
483-  apply ClosTrans.t_trans
484-  . apply ClosTrans.t_step; apply ParentOf.po_SC
485-  . apply ClosTrans.t_step; apply ParentOf.po_CM
486-
487--- Note to developers:
488---     HIDE: CH: A simple exercise could be nice here?
489-
490--- ### Example: Reflexive and Transitive Closure
491-
492--- As another example, the *reflexive and transitive closure*
493--- of a relation `R` is the smallest relation that contains `R`
494--- and that is reflexive and transitive. This can be defined by
495--- the following three rules (where we added a reflexivity rule
496--- to `ClosTrans`):
497-
498---                      R x y
499---              --------------------- (rt_step)
500---              ClosReflTrans R x y
501-
502---              --------------------- (rt_refl)
503---              ClosReflTrans R x x
504-
505---      ClosReflTrans R x y    ClosReflTrans R y z
506---   ---------------------------------------------- (rt_trans)
507---              ClosReflTrans R x z
508-
509-inductive ClosReflTrans {α: Type} (R: α → α → Prop) : α → α → Prop where
510-  | rt_step (x y : α) :
511-      R x y →
512-      ClosReflTrans R x y
513-  | rt_refl (x : α) :
514-      ClosReflTrans R x x
515-  | rt_trans (x y z : α) :
516-      ClosReflTrans R x y →
517-      ClosReflTrans R y z →
518-      ClosReflTrans R x z
519-
520--- For instance, this enables an equivalent definition of the
521--- Collatz conjecture. First we define a binary relation
522--- corresponding to the "Collatz step function" `csf`:
523-
524-def cs (n m : Nat) : Prop := csf n = m
525-
526--- This Collatz step relation can be used in conjunction with
527--- the reflexive and transitive closure operation to define a
528--- *Collatz multi-step* (`cms`) relation, expressing that a
529--- number `n` reaches another number `m` in zero or more
530--- Collatz steps:
531-
532-def cms (n m : Nat) : Prop := ClosReflTrans cs n m
533-def collatz' : Prop := ∀ (n : Nat), n ≠ 0 → cms n 1
534-
535--- Note to developers:
536---     HIDE: CH: Would it be helpful to add an exercise later
537---     proving cms equivalent to CollatzHoldsFor
538-
539--- Example: Permutations
540-
541--- The familiar mathematical concept of *permutation* also has
542--- an elegant formulation as an inductive relation. For
543--- simplicity, let's focus on permutations of lists with
544--- exactly three elements.
545-
546--- We can define such permutations by the following rules:
547-
548---      ------------------------- (perm3_swap12)
549---      Perm3 [a, b, c] [b, a, c]
550-
551---      ------------------------- (perm3_swap23)
552---      Perm3 [a, b, c] [a, c, b]
553-
554---   Perm3 l₁ l₂       Perm3 l₂ l₃
555---   ----------------------------- (perm3_trans)
556---            Perm3 l₁ l₃
557-
558--- For instance we can derive `Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [3, 2, 1]` as
559--- follows:
560-
561---   ─────────────────────────(perm3_swap12)   ─────────────────────────(perm3_swap23)
562---   Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [2, 1, 3]                 Perm3 [2, 1, 3] [2, 3, 1]
563---   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────(perm3_trans)   ─────────────────────────(perm3_swap12)
564---   Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [2, 3, 1]                                          Perm3 [2, 3, 1] [3, 2, 1]
565---   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────(perm3_trans)
566---   Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [3, 2, 1]
567-
568--- In Lean, we can define `Perm3` as follows:
569-
570-inductive Perm3 {α : Type} : List α → List α → Prop where
571-  | perm3_swap12 (a b c : α) :
572-      Perm3 [a, b, c] [b, a, c]
573-  | perm3_swap23 (a b c : α) :
574-      Perm3 [a, b, c] [a, c, b]
575-  | perm3_trans (l₁ l₂ l₃ : List α) :
576-      Perm3 l₁ l₂ → Perm3 l₂ l₃ → Perm3 l₁ l₃
577-
578--- ### Example: Evenness (yet again)
579-
580--- We've already seen two ways of stating a proposition that a
581--- number `n` is even: We can say
582-
583--- (1) `even n = true` (using the recursive boolean function
584--- `even`), or
585-
586--- (2) `∃ k, n = double k` (using an existential quantifier).
587-
588--- A third possibility, which we'll use as a simple running
589--- example in this chapter, is to say that a number is even if
590--- we can *establish* its evenness from the following two
591--- rules:
592-
593---       ---- (ev_0)
594---       Ev 0
595-
596---       Ev n
597---   ------------ (ev_succ_succ)
598---   Ev (n + 2)
599-
600--- To illustrate how this new definition of evenness works,
601--- let's imagine using it to show that `4` is even:
602-
603---           ———— (ev_0)
604---           Ev 0
605---       ———————————— (`ev_succ_succ`)
606---       Ev (S (S 0))
607---   ———————————————————— (`ev_succ_succ`)
608---   Ev (S (S (S (S 0))))
609-
610--- We can translate the informal definition of evenness from
611--- above into a formal `inductive` declaration, where each "way
612--- that a number can be even" corresponds to a separate
613--- constructor:
614-
615-inductive Ev : Nat → Prop where
616-  | ev_0                       : Ev 0
617-  | ev_succ_succ (n : Nat) (H : Ev n) : Ev (n + 2)
618-
619--- There are both similarities and a few differences between
620--- inductive *properties* like `Ev` and the inductive *types*
621--- like `Nat` or `List` that we have been using throughout the
622--- course:
623-
624---   inductive List (α:Type) : Type where
625---     | nil                       : List α
626---     | cons (x : α) (l : List α) : List α.
627-
628--- The most important difference is that the constructors of
629--- `Ev`, `ev_0` and `ev_succ_succ`, yield different types
630--- (`Ev 0` and `Ev (n + 2)`), whereas the `List` constructors
631--- both build `List α` values.
632-
633--- We can think of the inductive definition of `Ev` as defining
634--- a Lean property `Ev : Nat → Prop`, together with two
635--- "evidence constructors":
636-
637-#check (Ev.ev_0) -- Ev 0
638-#check Ev.ev_succ_succ -- ∀ (n : Nat) (H : Ev n) : Ev (n + 2)
639-
640--- These evidence constructors can be thought of as "primitive
641--- evidence of evenness", and they can be used later on just
642--- like proven theorems. In particular, we can use Lean's
643--- `apply` and `exact` tactics with the constructor names to
644--- obtain evidence for `Ev` of particular numbers...
645-
646-theorem ev_4 : Ev 4 := by
647-  apply Ev.ev_succ_succ; apply Ev.ev_succ_succ; exact Ev.ev_0
648-
649--- ... or we can use function application syntax to combine
650--- several constructors:
651-
652-theorem ev_4' : Ev 4 := by
653-  exact Ev.ev_succ_succ 2 (Ev.ev_succ_succ 0 Ev.ev_0)
654-
655--- ... or we can also use the `constructor` tactic we saw
656--- earlier to select the appropriate inductive constructor
657-
658-theorem ev_4'' : Ev 4 := by
659-  constructor; constructor; constructor
660-
661--- In this way, we can also prove theorems that have hypotheses
662--- involving `Ev`.
663-
664-theorem ev_plus4 (n : Nat) (h : Ev n) : Ev (4 + n) := by
665-  rw [Nat.add_comm]
666-  exact (Ev.ev_succ_succ _ (Ev.ev_succ_succ _ h))
667-
668--- ### Constructing Evidence for Permutations
669-
670--- Similarly we can apply the evidence constructors to obtain
671--- evidence of `Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [3, 2, 1]`:
672-
673-theorem Perm3_rev : Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [3, 2, 1] := by
674-  apply Perm3.perm3_trans (l₂:= [2, 3, 1])
675-  . apply Perm3.perm3_trans (l₂:=[2, 1, 3])
676-    . apply Perm3.perm3_swap12
677-    . apply Perm3.perm3_swap23
678-  . apply Perm3.perm3_swap12
679-
680--- And again we can equivalently use function application
681--- syntax to combine several constructors. (Note that the Lean
682--- type checker can infer not only types, but also Nats and
683--- List, when they are clear from the context.)
684-
685-theorem Perm3_rev' : Perm3 [1, 2, 3] [3, 2, 1] := by
686-  exact (Perm3.perm3_trans _ [2, 3, 1] _
687-          (Perm3.perm3_trans _ [2, 1, 3] _
688-            (Perm3.perm3_swap12 _ _ _)
689-            (Perm3.perm3_swap23 _ _ _))
690-          (Perm3.perm3_swap12 _ _ _))
691-
692--- So the informal derivation trees we drew above are not too
693--- far from what's happening formally. Formally we're using the
694--- evidence constructors to build *evidence trees*, similar to
695--- the finite trees we built using the constructors of data
696--- types such as Nat, List, binary trees, etc.
697-
698--- ## Using Evidence in Proofs
699-
700--- Besides *constructing* evidence that numbers are even, we
701--- can also *destruct* such evidence, reasoning about how it
702--- could have been built.
703-
704--- Defining `Ev` with an `inductive` declaration tells Lean not
705--- only that the constructors `ev_0` and `ev_succ_succ` are
706--- valid ways to build evidence that some number is `Ev`, but
707--- also that these two constructors are the *only* ways to
708--- build evidence that numbers are `Ev`.
709-
710--- In other words, if someone gives us evidence `E` for the
711--- proposition `Ev n`, then we know that `E` must be one of two
712--- things:
713-
714--- - `E = ev_0` and `n = 0`, or
715-
716--- - `E = ev_succ_succ n' E'` and `n = n' + 2`, where `E'` is
717---   evidence for `Ev n'`.
718-
719--- This suggests that it should be possible to do *case
720--- analysis* and even *induction* on evidence of evenness...
721-
722--- ### Destructing and Inverting Evidence
723-
724--- We can prove our characterization of evidence for `Ev n`,
725--- using `cases`.
726-
727-theorem ev_inversion : ∀ (n : Nat),
728-    Ev n →
729-    (n = 0) ∨ ∃ n', n = n' + 2 ∧ Ev n' := by
730-    intro n H
731-    cases H
732-    case ev_0 =>
733-      left; rfl
734-    case ev_succ_succ n H =>
735-      right; exists n
736-
737--- Facts like this are often called "inversion lemmas" because
738--- they allow us to "invert" some given information to reason
739--- about all the different ways it could have been derived.
740-
741--- We can use the inversion lemma that we proved above to help
742--- structure proofs:
743-
744-theorem ev_succ_succ_ev : ∀ n, Ev (n + 2) → Ev n := by
745-  intro n H
746-  apply ev_inversion at H
747-  cases H
748-  case inl _ => contradiction
749-  case inr h =>
750-    let ⟨n', ⟨h₁,  h₂⟩⟩ := h
751-    injections h₁ heq
752-    subst heq
753-    exact  h₂
754-
755--- We've provided a handy tactic called `inversion` that does
756--- the work of our inversion lemma and more besides.
757-
758-theorem ev_succ_succ_ev' : ∀ n, Ev (n + 2) → Ev n := by
759-  intro n h
760-  inversion h; assumption
761-
762--- We can use `inversion` to re-prove some theorems from
763--- `Tactics.lean`.
764-
765--- Note that `inversion` also works on equality propositions.
766-
767-theorem inversion_ex1 : ∀ (n m o : Nat),
768-  [n, m] = [o, o] → [n] = [m] := by
769-  intro n m o h
770-  inversion h; rfl
771-
772-theorem inversion_ex2 : ∀ (n : Nat),
773-  n + 1 = 0 → 2 + 2 = 5 := by
774-  intro n h
775-  inversion h
776-
777--- The `inversion` tactic works on any `H : P` where `P` is
778--- defined inductively:
779-
780--- - For each constructor of `P`, make a subgoal where `H` is
781---   constrained by the form of this constructor.
782-
783--- - Discard contradictory subgoals (such as `ev_0` above).
784-
785--- - Generate auxiliary equalities (as with `ev_succ_succ`
786---   above).
787-

789---     The wording there is totally awkward!

792--- our earlier notion (the one based on `double`).
793-

796-

852--- ### Induction on Evidence
853-
854--- If this story feels familiar, it is no coincidence: We
855--- encountered similar problems in the Induction chapter, when
856--- trying to use case analysis to prove results that required
857--- induction. And once again the solution is... induction!
858-
859--- Let's try proving that lemma again:
860-
861-theorem Nat.ev_Even : ∀ n, Ev n → Even n := by
862-  intro n h
863-  induction h
864-  /- h = ev_0 -/
865-  case ev_0 => exists 0  -- (`0 = double 0` is closed by `exists`'s final `rfl`)
866-  /- h = ev_succ_succ n' h',  with ih : Even n' -/
867-  case ev_succ_succ n' h' ih =>
868-    let ⟨k, hk⟩ := ih
869-    exists k + 1; rw [double_succ, hk]

185--- We need a bigger hammer: the *principle of induction* over
186--- natural numbers...
187-
188--- - If `P(n)` is some proposition involving a natural number
189---   `n`, and we want to show that `P` holds for *all* numbers,
190---   we can reason like this:
191-
192--- - show that `P(zero)` holds
193-
194--- - show that, if `P(n')` holds, then so does `P(succ n')`
195-
196--- - conclude that `P(n)` holds for all `n`.

209-      Then we can rewrite with the induction hypothesis.

233--- ### Tip: the `rw` tactic
234-
235--- As you've probably noticed, a common pattern in Lean proofs
236--- is `rewrite [...]` followed by `rfl`. There is a tactic that
237--- combines these two steps: `rw [...]` will automatically
238--- close the goal if the rewrite makes the goal true by
239--- definition. For example, instead of writing
240-
241---   rewrite [double_zero]; rfl
242-
243--- We could write this:
244-
245---   rw [double_zero]
246-
247--- If `rw` leaves a goal that looks definitionally true, try
248--- adding `rfl` after it.
249-
250--- ### Exercise (2 stars): double_add ⭐⭐
251-
252--- Consider the following function, which doubles its argument:
253-
254-def double (n : Nat) : Nat :=
255-  match n with
256-  | zero    => zero
257-  | succ n' => succ (succ (double n'))
258-
259-theorem double_zero : double zero = zero := by rfl
260-theorem double_succ n : double (succ n) = succ (succ (double n)) := by rfl
261-attribute [irreducible] double
262-

271--- New tactic: `have`.
272-
273-theorem mult_zero_add' (n m : Nat) :
274-    ((zero + n) + zero) * m = n * m := by
275-  have h : (zero + n) + zero = n := by
276-    rw [zero_add, add_zero]
277-  rw [h]
278-
279-sf_expect_failure
280-  example (n m p q : Nat) :
281-     (n + m) + (p + q) = (m + n) + (p + q) := by
282-    /-
283-      We just need to swap (n + m) for (m + n)... seems
284-      like add_comm should do the trick!
285-      But `rw [add_comm]` might rewrite the wrong `+`!
286-    -/
287-    rw [add_comm]
288-
289--- unsolved goals
290--- n m p q : Nat
291--- ⊢ p + q + (n + m) = m + n + (p + q)
292-
293--- To use `add_comm` at the point where we need it, we can
294--- supply explicit arguments: `rw [add_comm n m]` tells Lean
295--- exactly which `+` to rewrite. (We can also use `have` to
296--- establish the specific equation we want, then rewrite with
297--- it.)
298-
299-theorem add_rearrange (n m p q : Nat) :
300-    (n + m) + (p + q) = (m + n) + (p + q) := by
301-  rw [add_comm n m]

326--- ## More Exercises
327-
328--- Tip: By default, `rewrite` and `rw` rewrite left to right,
329--- i.e., they transform the hypothesis or goal being rewritten
330--- from the form on the left side of the equality to the right
331--- side. To rewrite from right to left, use `rewrite [← h]` or
332--- `rw [← h]`, where `←` is entered as `\l` or `\<-`.

402--- ### A New Tactic Combinator
403-
404--- New tactic combinator: `t₁ <;> t₂` runs `t₁`, then runs `t₂`
405--- on every subgoal produced by `t₁`.
406-
407-example (b : Bool) : (b || true) = true := by
408-  cases b <;> rfl
409-
410--- This is short for:
411-
412-example (b : Bool) : (b || true) = true := by
413-  cases b with
414-  | false => rfl
415-  | true  => rfl
416-
417--- We can also chain `<;>`s.
418-
419-example (b c : Bool) : (b && c) = (c && b) := by
420-  cases b <;> cases c <;> rfl

504--- ## Bin to Nat and Back to Bin (Advanced)
505-
506--- The opposite direction — starting with a `Bin`, converting
507--- to `Nat`, then converting back to `Bin` — turns out to be
508--- problematic. That is, the following "theorem" does not hold.
509-
510-sf_expect_failure
511-  example (b : Bin) : natToBin (binToNat b) = b := by
512-
513--- Let's explore why this theorem fails and how to prove a
514--- modified version of it. We'll start with some lemmas that
515--- might seem unrelated but will turn out to be relevant.
516-

518-

520--- the chapter.
521-
522-theorem double_incr (n : Nat) :
523-    double (succ n) = (double n) + two := by
524-  sorry
525-
526--- Now define a similar doubling function for `Bin`.
527-
528-def doubleBin (b : Bin) : Bin := sorry
529-
530--- Fill in the characterizing lemmas for this definition below:
531-
532--- FILL IN HERE
533-
534--- Check that your function correctly doubles zero.
535-
536-theorem double_bin_zero : doubleBin .z = .z := sorry
537-
538--- Prove this lemma, which corresponds to `double_incr`.
539-
540-theorem double_incr_bin (b : Bin) :
541-    doubleBin (incr b) = incr (incr (doubleBin b)) := by
542-  sorry
543-
544--- Let's return to our desired theorem:
545-
546-sf_expect_failure
547-  example (b : Bin) : natToBin (binToNat b) = b := by
548-
549--- The theorem fails because there are some `Bin` such that we
550--- won't necessarily get back to the *original* `Bin`, but
551--- instead to an "equivalent" `Bin`. (We deliberately leave
552--- that notion undefined here for you to think about.)
553-
554--- Explain in a comment, below, why this failure occurs. Your
555--- explanation will not be graded, but it's important that you
556--- get it clear in your mind before going on to the next part.
557--- If you're stuck on this, think about alternative
558--- implementations of `doubleBin` that might have failed to
559--- satisfy `double_bin_zero` yet otherwise seem correct.
560-
561--- To solve that problem, we can introduce a *normalization*
562--- function that selects the simplest `Bin` out of all the
563--- equivalent `Bin`. Then we can prove that the conversion from
564--- `Bin` to `Nat` and back again produces that normalized,
565--- simplest `Bin`.
566-

1-import LF.Induction
2-import LF.UsingLean

4-import LF.SFLCompat
5-
6--- # Lists: Working with Structured Data
7-
8-namespace Lists
9-
10--- Note to developers (before next release):
11---     Note that rewrite laws should sometimes differ from
12---     pattern matching now
13-
14--- ## Pairs of Numbers
15-
16--- An inductive definition of pairs of numbers. It has just one
17--- constructor, taking two arguments:
18-
19-inductive NatProd where
20-  | pair (n1 n2 : Nat)
21-
22-#check (NatProd.pair 3 5)
23-
24--- Functions for extracting the first and second components of
25--- a pair can then be defined by pattern matching.
26-
27-def NatProd.fst (p : NatProd) : Nat :=
28-  match p with
29-  | .pair x _ => x
30-
31-def NatProd.snd (p : NatProd) : Nat :=
32-  match p with
33-  | .pair _ y => y
34-
35--- Defining these functions with the `NatProd` type name
36--- qualifying their name allows us to use them with `.`
37--- notation:
38-
39-example : (NatProd.pair 3 5).fst = 3 := by rfl
40-
41--- A nicer notation for pairs:
42-
43-example : (⟨3, 5⟩ : NatProd).fst = 3 := by rfl
44-
45--- The anonymous constructor can be used in both expressions
46--- and in pattern matches.
47-
48-def NatProd.fst' (p : NatProd) : Nat :=
49-  match p with
50-  | ⟨x, _⟩ => x
51-
52-def NatProd.snd' (p : NatProd) : Nat :=
53-  match p with
54-  | ⟨_, y⟩ => y
55-
56-def NatProd.swap (p : NatProd) : NatProd :=
57-  ⟨snd p, fst p⟩
58-
59--- Lean also provides a convenient way to define `inductive`
60--- structures like pairs that have a single constructor but
61--- multiple ways to access their data, using the `structure`
62--- keyword. The definition of `NatProd'` below is equivalent to
63--- the `NatProd` definition from earlier, except that Lean
64--- automatically generates the `fst` and `snd` accessors.
65-
66-structure NatProd' where
67-  fst : Nat
68-  snd : Nat
69-
70-#check (NatProd'.mk 3 5)
71-example : (NatProd'.mk 3 5).fst = 3 := by rfl
72-example : (⟨3, 5⟩ : NatProd').fst = 3 := by rfl
73-
74--- To expose the structure of a pair, use `cases` (or
75--- destructuring).
76-
77-theorem surjective_pairing : ∀ p : NatProd,
78-    p = ⟨p.fst, p.snd⟩ := by
79-  intro ⟨n, m⟩; rfl
80-
81-theorem surjective_pairing_cases (p : NatProd) :
82-    p = ⟨p.fst, p.snd⟩ := by
83-  cases p; rfl
84-
85--- ## Lists of Numbers
86-
87--- An inductive definition of *lists* of numbers:
88-
89-inductive NatList : Type where
90-  | nil
91-  | cons (n : Nat) (l : NatList)

93--- By convention, we place the operations (functions) of an
94--- inductive type inside the namespace implicitly created by
95--- that type's definition.
96-
97-namespace NatList
98-
99--- Some notation for lists to make our lives easier:
100-
101--- Don't worry too much about what this is doing:
102-
103-scoped infixr:65 (priority := high) " :: " => cons
104-scoped macro (priority := high) "[" elems:term,* "]" : term => do
105-  elems.getElems.foldrM (``(cons $(⟨·⟩) $(⟨·⟩))) (← ``(nil))
106-
107-@[scoped app_unexpander nil]
108-def unexpandNil : Lean.PrettyPrinter.Unexpander
109-  | `($_) => `([])
110-
111-@[scoped app_unexpander cons]
112-def unexpandCons : Lean.PrettyPrinter.Unexpander
113-  | `($_ $x []) => `([$x])
114-  | `($_ $x [$xs,*]) => `([$x, $xs,*])
115-  | _ => throw ()
116-
117--- We first define `::` as right-associative *notation* for
118--- `cons`, and then define list notation *macro* with
119--- *unexpander*, allowing us to write `[1, 2]` instead of
120--- `1 :: 2 :: []`.
121-
122--- Now these all mean exactly the same thing:
123-
124-def mylist1 : NatList := 1 :: (2 :: (3 :: []))
125-def mylist2 : NatList := 1 :: 2 :: 3 :: []
126-def mylist3 : NatList := [1, 2, 3]

130--- ### Repeat
131-
132-def myRepeat (n count : Nat) : NatList :=
133-  match count with
134-  | 0 => []
135-  | count' + 1 => n :: myRepeat n count'
136-
137--- Some simple facts about repetition:
138-
139-theorem repeat_zero {v : Nat} : myRepeat v 0 = [] := rfl
140-
141-theorem repeat_succ {v count : Nat} : myRepeat v (count + 1) = v :: myRepeat v count := rfl
142-
143-def length (l : NatList) : Nat :=
144-  match l with
145-  | [] => 0
146-  | _ :: t => (length t) + 1
147-
148--- Some simple facts about list lengths:
149-
150-theorem length_nil : [].length = 0 := rfl
151-
152-theorem length_cons {n : Nat} {l : NatList} : (n :: l).length = l.length + 1 := rfl

157-  match l1 with
158-  | [] => l2
159-  | h :: t => h :: append t l2

415--- ## Reasoning About Lists
416-
417--- As with numbers, some proofs about list functions need only
418--- rewriting...
419-
420--- ...and some need case analysis.
421-
422-theorem tail_length_pred (l : NatList) :
423-    l.length.pred = l.tail.length := by
424-  cases l with
425-  | nil       => rw [tail_nil, length_nil]; dsimp
426-  | cons n l' => rw [tail_cons, length_cons]; dsimp
427-
428--- Usually, though, interesting theorems about lists require
429--- induction for their proofs. We'll see how to do this next.
430-
431--- ### Induction on Lists
432-
433--- Lean generates an induction principle for every `inductive`
434--- definition, including lists. We can use the `induction`
435--- tactic on lists to prove things like the associativity of
436--- list-append...
437-
438-theorem append_assoc (l1 l2 l3 : NatList) :
439-    (l1 ++ l2) ++ l3 = l1 ++ (l2 ++ l3) := by
440-  induction l1 with
441-  | nil =>
442-    rw [nil_append, nil_append]
443-  | cons n l1' ih =>
444-    rw [cons_append, cons_append, cons_append, ih]
445-
446--- For comparison, here is an informal proof of the same
447--- theorem.
448-
449--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
450---     Are we going to consistently write Qed at the end of
451---     proofs? We should agree on a convention.
452-
453--- *Theorem*: For all lists `l1`, `l2`, and `l3`,
454-
455---   (l1 ++ l2) ++ l3 = l1 ++ (l2 ++ l3).
456-
457--- *Proof*: By induction on `l1`.
458-
459--- - First, suppose `l1 = []`. We must show
460-
461---   ([] ++ l2) ++ l3 = [] ++ (l2 ++ l3),
462-
463--- which follows directly from the definition of `append`.
464-
465--- - Next, suppose `l1 = n :: l1'`, with
466-
467---   (l1' ++ l2) ++ l3 = l1' ++ (l2 ++ l3)
468-
469--- (the induction hypothesis). We must show
470-
471---   ((n :: l1') ++ l2) ++ l3 = (n :: l1') ++ (l2 ++ l3).
472-
473--- By the definition of `append`, this follows from
474-
475---   n :: ((l1' ++ l2) ++ l3) = n :: (l1' ++ (l2 ++ l3)),
476-
477--- which is immediate from the induction hypothesis. *Qed*.
478-
479--- #### Generalizing Statements
480-
481--- Sometimes statements need to be generalized to prove them by
482--- induction:
483-
484-sf_expect_failure
485-  theorem myRepeat_append {c n : Nat} :
486-      myRepeat n c ++ myRepeat n c = myRepeat n (c + c) := by
487-    induction c with
488-    | zero => rw [repeat_zero, nil_append]
489-    | succ c' ih =>
490-      rw [repeat_succ]
491-      -- Now we seem to be stuck.
492-      -- The `ih` only works for `c' + c'`,
493-      -- but we need `c' + 1 + (c' + 1)`.
494-
495--- unsolved goals
496--- case succ
497--- n c' : Nat
498--- ih : myRepeat n c' ++ myRepeat n c' = myRepeat n (c' + c')
499--- ⊢ (n :: myRepeat n c') ++ (n :: myRepeat n c') = myRepeat n (c' + 1 + (c' + 1))
500-
501--- A generalization that gives a stronger inductive hypothesis:
502-
503-theorem myRepeat_append {c₁ c₂ n : Nat} :
504-    myRepeat n c₁ ++ myRepeat n c₂ = myRepeat n (c₁ + c₂) := by
505-  induction c₁ with
506-  | zero =>
507-    rw [repeat_zero, Nat.zero_add, nil_append]
508-  | succ c1' ih =>
509-    rw [Nat.succ_add, repeat_succ, repeat_succ, cons_append, ih]
510-
511--- #### Reversing a List
512-
513--- A more interesting example of induction over lists:
514-
515-def reverse (l : NatList) : NatList :=
516-  match l with
517-  | [] => []
518-  | h :: t => t.reverse ++ [h]
519-
520-theorem reverse_nil : [].reverse = [] := by rfl
521-
522-theorem reverse_cons {h : Nat} {t : NatList} : (h :: t).reverse = t.reverse ++ [h] := by rfl
523-
524-example : [1, 2, 3].reverse = [3, 2, 1] := by rfl
525-
526-example : [].reverse = [] := by rfl
527-
528--- Let's try to prove
529--- `∀ l : NatList, length (reverse l) = length l`.
530-
531-sf_expect_failure
532-  example (l : NatList) :
533-      l.reverse.length = l.length := by
534-    induction l with
535-    | nil => rw [reverse_nil]
536-    | cons n l' ih =>
537-      rw [reverse_cons]
538-      -- Now we seem to be stuck: the goal involves `++`,
539-      -- but we don't have any useful equations
540-      -- in either the immediate context or in the global
541-      -- environment!
542-
543--- unsolved goals
544--- case cons
545--- n : Nat
546--- l' : NatList
547--- ih : l'.reverse.length = l'.length
548--- ⊢ (l'.reverse ++ [n]).length = (n :: l').length
549-
550-sf_expect_failure
551-  theorem length_append_succ {l : NatList} {n : Nat} :
552-      (l.reverse ++ [n]).length = l.reverse.length + 1 := by
553-    induction l with
554-    | nil =>
555-      rw [reverse_nil, nil_append, length_cons, length_nil]
556-    | cons m l' ih =>
557-      rw [reverse_cons]
558-      -- `ih` not applicable
559-
560--- unsolved goals
561--- case cons
562--- n m : Nat
563--- l' : NatList
564--- ih : (l'.reverse ++ [n]).length = l'.reverse.length + 1
565--- ⊢ (l'.reverse ++ [m] ++ [n]).length = (l'.reverse ++ [m]).length + 1
566-
567-theorem append_length_succ (l : NatList) (n : Nat) :
568-    (l ++ [n]).length = l.length + 1 := by
569-  induction l with
570-  | nil => rw [nil_append, length_cons]
571-  | cons m l' ih =>
572-    rw [cons_append, length_cons, ih, length_cons]
573-
574--- Now we can prove the main theorem.
575-
576-theorem length_reverse {l : NatList} :
577-    l.reverse.length = l.length := by
578-  induction l with
579-  | nil => rw [reverse_nil]
580-  | cons n l' ih =>
581-    rw [reverse_cons, append_length_succ, ih, length_cons]
582-
583-theorem length_append {l₁ l₂ : NatList} :
584-    (l₁ ++ l₂).length = l₁.length + l₂.length := by
585-  sorry

630-open NatList
631-
632--- ## Options
633-
634--- Suppose we'd like a function to retrieve the `n`th element
635--- of a list. What to do if the list is too short?
636-
637-def nthBad (l : NatList) (n : Nat) : Nat :=
638-  match l with
639-  | [] => 42
640-  | a :: l' => match n with
641-    | 0 => a
642-    | n' + 1 => nthBad l' n'
643-
644--- The solution: return a `NatOption`.
645-
646-end NatList
647-
648-inductive NatOption : Type where
649-  | some (n : Nat)
650-  | none
651-
652-namespace NatList
653-
654-def nth? (l : NatList) (n : Nat) : NatOption :=
655-  match l with
656-  | [] => .none
657-  | a :: l' => match n with
658-    | 0 => .some a
659-    | n' + 1 => nth? l' n'
660-
661-example : nth? [4, 5, 6, 7] 0 = .some 4 := by rfl
662-example : nth? [4, 5, 6, 7] 3 = .some 7 := by rfl
663-example : nth? [4, 5, 6, 7] 9 = .none := by rfl
664-
665-def NatOption.elim (d : Nat) (o : NatOption) : Nat :=
666-  match o with
667-  | .some n => n
668-  | .none => d
669-
670-theorem NatOption.elim_none {d : Nat} : elim d .none = d := by rfl
671-
672-theorem NatOption.elim_some {d₁ d₂ : Nat} : elim d₁ (.some d₂) = d₂ := by rfl
673-
674-end NatList
675-
676--- ## Partial Maps
677-
678--- As a final illustration of how data structures can be
679--- defined in Lean, here is a simple *partial map* data type,
680--- analogous to the map or dictionary data structures found in
681--- most programming languages.
682-
683--- First, we define a new type `MyId` to serve as the "keys" of
684--- our partial maps.
685-
686-structure MyId where
687-  val : Nat
688-
689--- Internally, a `MyId` is just a number. Introducing a
690--- separate type by wrapping each `Nat` makes definitions more
691--- readable and gives us flexibility to change representations
692--- later if we want to.
693-
694--- We'll also need an equality test for `MyId`s:
695-
696-def MyId.beq (x₁ x₂ : MyId) : Bool :=
697-  x₁.val == x₂.val
698-
699--- ### Exercise (1 star): MyId.beq_refl ⭐
700-
701-theorem MyId.beq_refl (x : MyId) : MyId.beq x x = true := by
702-  sorry
703-
704--- Now we define the type of partial maps:
705-
706-inductive PartialMap : Type where
707-  | empty : PartialMap
708-  | record (i : MyId) (v : Nat) (m : PartialMap) : PartialMap
709-
710-namespace PartialMap
711-
712--- The `update` function overrides the entry for a given key in
713--- a partial map by shadowing it with a new one (or simply adds
714--- a new entry if the given key is not already present).
715-
716-def update (d : PartialMap) (x : MyId) (value : Nat) : PartialMap :=
717-  record x value d
718-
719--- We can define functions on `PartialMap`s by pattern
720--- matching.
721-
722-def find (x : MyId) (d : PartialMap) : NatOption :=
723-  match d with
724-  | empty => .none
725-  | record y v d' =>
726-    bif MyId.beq x y then .some v
727-    else find x d'

734-    find x (update d x v) = .some v := by

9--- # Logic in Lean
10-
11--- Note to developers (before next release):
12---     Unlike earlier chapters, there are probably too many
13---     WORKINCLASSes in this chapter. BCP 20: But conversely
14---     some more quizzes would be great!
15-
16--- So far, we have seen:
17-
18--- - *propositions*: mathematical statements, so far only of 3
19---   kinds:
20-
21---   - equality propositions (`e1 = e2`)
22---   - implications (`a -> b`)
23---   - quantified propositions (`∀ x, a`)
24-
25--- - *proofs*: ways of presenting evidence for the truth of a
26---   proposition
27-
28--- In this chapter we will introduce several more flavors of
29--- both propositions and proofs.
30-
31--- Like everything in Lean, well-formed propositions have a
32--- *type*:
33-
34--- ## The `Prop` Type
35-
36-#check (∀ n m : Nat, n + m = m + n : Prop)
37-
38--- Note that *all* syntactically well-formed propositions have
39--- type `Prop` in Lean, regardless of whether they are true or
40--- not.
41-
42--- Simply *being* a proposition is one thing; being *provable*
43--- is a different thing!
44-
45-#check (2 = 2 : Prop)
46-#check (3 = 2 : Prop)
47-#check (∀ n : Nat, n = 2 : Prop)
48-
49--- So far, we've seen one primary place where propositions can
50--- appear: in `theorem` declarations.
51-
52-theorem plus_2_2_is_4 : 2 + 2 = 4 := rfl
53-
54--- Propositions are first-class entities. For example, we can
55--- name them:
56-
57-def PlusClaim : Prop := 2 + 2 = 4
58-
59-#check PlusClaim
60-
61--- PlusClaim : Prop
62-
63-theorem plusClaim_is_true : PlusClaim := rfl
64-
65--- We can also write *parameterized* propositions — that is,
66--- functions that take arguments of some type and return a
67--- proposition.
68-
69-def Nat.IsThree (n : Nat) : Prop := n = 3
70-
71-#check (Nat.IsThree)
72-
73--- Nat.IsThree : Nat → Prop
74-
75--- In Lean, functions that return propositions are said to
76--- define *properties* of their arguments.
77-
78--- For instance, here's a (polymorphic) property defining the
79--- familiar notion of an *injective function*.
80-
81-def Injective {α β : Type} (f : α → β) : Prop :=
82-  ∀ x y : α, f x = f y → x = y
83-
84-theorem succ_inj' : Injective Nat.succ := by
85-  intro x y h
86-  injection h
87-
88--- The familiar equality operator `=` is a (binary) function
89--- that returns a `Prop`. The expression `n = m` is notation
90--- for `Eq n m`. Because `Eq` can be used with elements of any
91--- type, it is also polymorphic:
92-
93-#check Eq
94-
95--- Eq.{u_1} {α : Sort u_1} : α → α → Prop
96-
97--- As a convenience, Lean will cast booleans by equating them
98--- to `true`, which is why checking them against `Prop`
99--- succeeds. It also casts boolean equalities to propositions
100--- by equating to `true`, and boolean inequalities by equating
101--- to `false`. For clarity, we will avoid relying on these
102--- implicit casts.
103-
104-#check (false : Prop)
105-
106--- false = true : Prop
107-
108-#check (true : Prop)
109-
110--- true = true : Prop
111-

115-

117-

120--- 3. `∀ n : Nat, Prop`
121--- 4. `Nat → Nat`
122--- 5. Not typeable
123-

127-
128---   ∀ n : Nat, (n + 1).pred = n

132--- 3. `∀ n : Nat, Prop`
133--- 4. `Nat → Nat`
134--- 5. Not typeable
135-

139-
140---   ∀ n : Nat, n.pred + 1
141-
142--- 1. `Prop`
143--- 2. `Nat → Prop`
144--- 3. `∀ n : Nat, Prop`
145--- 4. `Nat → Nat`
146--- 5. Not typeable
147-

151-
152---   fun n : Nat => n.pred + 1
153-
154--- 1. `Prop`
155--- 2. `Nat → Prop`
156--- 3. `∀ n : Nat, Prop`

163-

172--- _Quiz:_
173-
174--- Which of the following is *not* a proposition?
175-
176--- 1. `3 + 2 = 4`
177--- 2. `3 + 2 = 5`
178--- 3. `3 + 2 == 5`
179--- 4. `(3 + 2 == 4) = false`
180--- 5. `∀ n, (3 + 2 == n) = true → n = 5`
181--- 6. All of these are propositions
182-
183--- ## Logical Connectives
184-
185--- ### Conjunction
186-
187--- The *conjunction*, or *logical and*, of propositions `a` and
188--- `b` is written `a ∧ b`; it represents the claim that both
189--- `a` and `b` are true.
190-
191-example : 3 + 4 = 7 ∧ 2 * 2 = 4 := by
192-  /- A proof of a conjunction is a pair of proofs of the two components.
193-      To prove a conjunction, we build a pair using `constructor`. -/
194-  constructor
195-  · rfl /- 3 + 4 = 7 -/
196-  · rfl /- 2 * 2 = 4 -/
197-
198--- The constructor for conjunction is `And.intro`, which
199--- concludes that `a ∧ b` given that `a` and `b` hold
200--- individually.
201-
202-#check And.intro
203-
204--- And.intro {a b : Prop} (left : a) (right : b) : a ∧ b
205-
206--- We can also apply the constructor for the conjunction
207--- explicitly.
208-
209-example : 3 + 4 = 7 ∧ 2 * 2 = 4 := by
210-  apply And.intro
211-  · rfl /- 3 + 4 = 7 -/
212-  · rfl /- 2 * 2 = 4 -/
213-
214--- Rather than applying the constructor, we can explicitly
215--- provide the arguments to the constructor as an `exact`
216--- proof.
217-
218-example : 3 + 4 = 7 ∧ 2 * 2 = 4 := by
219-  exact And.intro rfl rfl
220-
221--- We can also use Lean's anonymous constructor notation
222--- `⟨..., ...⟩`, which works on constructors for proofs as
223--- well.
224-
225-example : 3 + 4 = 7 ∧ 2 * 2 = 4 := by
226-  exact ⟨rfl, rfl⟩
227-
228--- So much for proving conjunctive statements. To go in the
229--- other direction — i.e., to *use* a conjunctive hypothesis to
230--- help prove something else — we can use `obtain` to obtain
231--- the components.
232-
233-example (n m : Nat) : n = 0 ∧ m = 0 → n + m = 0 := by
234-  sorry
235-
236--- We can also match on `h` right at the point where we
237--- introduce it, instead of introducing and then destructing
238--- it:
239-
240-example (n m : Nat) : n = 0 ∧ m = 0 → n + m = 0 := by
241-  intro ⟨hn, hm⟩
242-  rw [hn, hm]
243-
244--- For the present example, both ways work. But in other
245--- situations, we may wind up with a conjunctive hypothesis in
246--- the middle of a proof...
247-
248-example (n m : Nat) (h : n + m = 0) : n * m = 0 := by
249-  sorry
250-
251--- The infix notation `∧` is actually just syntactic sugar for
252--- `And a b`. That is, `And` is a Lean operator that takes two
253--- propositions as arguments and yields a proposition.
254-
255-#check And
256-
257--- And (a b : Prop) : Prop
258-
259--- ### Disjunction
260-
261--- Another important connective is the *disjunction*, or
262--- *logical or*, of two propositions: `a ∨ b` is true when
263--- either `a` or lean`b` is. This infix notation stands for
264--- `Or a b`, where `Or : Prop -> Prop -> Prop`.
265-
266--- To use a disjunctive hypothesis in a proof, we proceed by
267--- case analysis — which, as with other data types like `Nat`,
268--- is done using `cases`. The two cases are `inl` (for "left
269--- injection", or "in the left case") and `inr` (for "right
270--- injection", or "in the right case").
271-
272-theorem Nat.factor_is_zero (n m : Nat) (h : n = 0 ∨ m = 0) : n * m = 0 := by
273-  cases h with
274-  /- `n = 0` -/
275-  | inl hn => rw [hn, Nat.zero_mul]
276-  /- `m = 0` -/
277-  | inr hm => rw [hm, Nat.mul_zero]
278-
279--- Rather than performing case analysis via `cases`, we can
280--- also use `obtain` to match on the two possible injections,
281--- much like with `obtain` and `∧`.
282-
283-theorem and_is_false (b1 b2 : Bool) (h : (b1 = false) ∨ (b2 = false)) :
284-    (b1 && b2) = false := by
285-  obtain hb1 | hb2 := h
286-  · rw [hb1, Bool.false_and]
287-  · rw [hb2, Bool.and_false]
288-
289--- Conversely, to show that a disjunction holds, it suffices to
290--- show that one of its sides holds. This can be done via the
291--- tactics `left` and `right`. As their names imply, the first
292--- one requires proving the left side of the disjunction, while
293--- the second requires proving the right side. Here is a
294--- trivial use...
295-
296-theorem or_intro_l (a b : Prop) (h : a) : a ∨ b := by
297-  left; exact h
298-
299--- ... and here is a slightly more interesting example
300--- requiring both `left` and `right`:
301-
302-theorem Nat.zero_or_succ (n : Nat) : n = 0 ∨ n = (n + 1).pred := by
303-  sorry
304-
305--- ### Exercise (2 stars): mul_is_zero ⭐⭐
306-
307-theorem Nat.mul_is_zero (n m : Nat) (h : n * m = 0) : n = 0 ∨ m = 0 := by
308-  sorry
309-
310--- ### Exercise (1 star): or_commute ⭐
311-
312-theorem or_commute (a b : Prop) (h : a ∨ b) : b ∨ a := by
313-  sorry
314-
315--- ### Falsehood and Negation
316-
317--- Up to this point, we have mostly been concerned with proving
318--- "positive" statements — addition is commutative, appending
319--- lists is associative, etc. We are sometimes also interested
320--- in negative results, demonstrating that some proposition is
321--- *not* true. Such statements are expressed with the logical
322--- negation operator `¬`, which a prefix notation for `Not`.
323-
324--- To see how negation works, recall the *principle of
325--- explosion* from the `Tactics` chapter, which asserts that,
326--- if we assume a contradiction, then any other proposition can
327--- be derived.
328-
329--- Following this intuition, we could define `¬ a` ("not `a`")
330--- as `∀ c, a → c`. Lean makes an equivalent but slightly
331--- different choice, defining `¬ a` as `a → False`, where
332--- `False` is a specific unprovable proposition defined in the
333--- standard library.
334-
335-#check Not
336-#print Not
337-
338-example (a : Prop) : Not a = (a → False) := rfl
339-example (a : Prop) : (¬ a) = (a → False) := rfl
340-
341--- Not (a : Prop) : Prop
342-
343--- def Not : Prop → Prop :=
344--- fun a => a → False
345-
346--- Since `False` is a contradictory proposition, the principle
347--- of explosion also applies to it. If we can get `False` into
348--- the context, we can use `cases` on it to complete any goal:
349-
350-theorem ex_falso_quodlibet (a : Prop) (h : False) : a := by
351-  cases h
352-
353--- Inequality is a very common form of negated statement, so
354--- there is a special notation for it: `≠`, which is infix
355--- notation for `Ne`.
356-
357-#print Ne
358-
359--- @[reducible] def Ne.{u} : {α : Sort u} → α → α → Prop :=
360--- fun {α} a b => ¬a = b
361-
362-theorem zero_not_one : 0 ≠ 1 := by
363-  /- The proposition `0 ≠ 1` is exactly the same as `¬ (0 = 1)`
364-      — that is, `Not (0 = 1)` — which unfolds to `(0 = 1) → False`. -/
365-  /- To prove an inequality, we may assume the opposite equality... -/
366-  intro contra
367-  /- ...and deduce a contradiction from it. Here, the equality
368-      `0 = 1` corresponds to `zero = succ zero`, which contradicts
369-      disjointness of constructors `zero` and `succ`, so `contradiction`
370-      takes care of it. -/
371-  contradiction
372-
373--- It takes a little practice to get used to working with
374--- negation in Lean. Even though *you* may see perfectly well
375--- why a claim involving negation holds, it can be a little
376--- tricky at first to see how to make Lean understand it!
377-
378--- Here are proofs of a few familiar facts to help get you
379--- warmed up.
380-
381-theorem not_False : ¬ False := by
382-  intro h; exact h
383-
384-theorem contradiction_implies_anything (a b : Prop) (h : a ∧ ¬ a) : b := by
385-  sorry
386-
387-theorem double_neg (a : Prop) (ha : a) : ¬ ¬ a := by
388-  sorry
389-
390--- Since inequality involves a negation, getting comfortable
391--- with it also often requires a little practice.
392-
393--- A useful trick: if you are trying to prove a nonsensical
394--- goal, apply `ex_falso_quodlibet` to change the goal to
395--- `False`. This makes it easier to use assumptions of the form
396--- `¬ a`, and in particular of the form `x ≠ y`.
397-
398-theorem not_true_is_false (b : Bool) (h : b ≠ true) : b = false := by
399-  cases b with
400-  | false => rfl
401-  | true =>
402-    dsimp [Ne, Not] at h
403-    apply ex_falso_quodlibet
404-    apply h
405-    rfl
406-

480--- ## Truth
481-
482--- Besides `False`, Lean's standard library also defines
483--- `True`, a proposition that is trivially true. To prove it,
484--- we use the constructor `True.intro` explicitly, or the
485--- anonymous constructor `⟨⟩`, or the `constructor` tactic.
486-
487-example : True := by exact True.intro
488-example : True := True.intro
489-example : True := by exact ⟨⟩
490-example : True := ⟨⟩
491-example : True := by constructor
492-
493--- Unlike `False`, which is used extensively, `True` is used
494--- relatively rarely: it is trivial (and therefore
495--- uninteresting) to prove as a goal, and it provides no useful
496--- information when it appears as a hypothesis.
497-
498--- ### Logical Equivalence
499-
500--- The handy "if and only if" connective, which asserts that
501--- two propositions have the same truth value, is a structure
502--- containing the two implication directions. `a ↔ b` is
503--- notation for `Iff a b`.
504-
505--- You can use `Iff.mp` to access the forward direction of the
506--- iff, `Iff.mpr` to access the backwards direction, and
507--- `Iff.intro` to convert a goal of the form `a ↔ b` to two
508--- goals of the form `a → b` and `b → a`.
509-
510-#check (fun α β : Prop => α ↔ β : Prop → Prop → Prop)
511-
512-#check Iff
513-#check Iff.intro
514-#check Iff.mp
515-#check Iff.mpr
516-
517--- Iff (a b : Prop) : Prop
518-
519--- Iff.intro {a b : Prop} (mp : a → b) (mpr : b → a) : a ↔ b
520-
521--- Iff.mp {a b : Prop} (self : a ↔ b) : a → b
522-
523--- Iff.mpr {a b : Prop} (self : a ↔ b) : b → a
524-
525-theorem iff_sym (a b : Prop) (h : a ↔ b) : b ↔ a := by
526-  sorry
527-
528-theorem not_true_iff_false (b : Bool) : b ≠ true ↔ b = false := by
529-  constructor
530-  · apply not_true_is_false
531-  · intro h; rw [h]; intro h'; contradiction
532-

539-  sorry

559--- ### Existential Quantification
560-
561-#check Exists
562-
563--- Exists.{u} {α : Sort u} (p : α → Prop) : Prop
564-
565-def Nat.Even x := ∃ n : Nat, x = Nat.double n
566-
567-#check (Nat.Even)
568-
569--- Nat.Even : Nat → Prop
570-
571-open Nat in
572-example : Even 4 := by exists 2
573-  -- `4 = double 2` holds by `rfl`,
574-  -- but is proven automatically by `exists`
575-
576--- Conversely, if we have an existential hypothesis `∃ x, a` in
577--- the context, can destrucure it to obtain a witness `x` and a
578--- hypothesis stating that `a` holds of `x`.
579-
580-example n : (∃ m, n = m + 4) → (∃ o, n = o + 2) := by
581-  intro ⟨m, hm⟩
582-  exists (m + 2)

584--- ## Recap: Logical Connectives in Lean
585-
586--- Connectives introduced in this chapter:
587-
588--- - `a ∧ b` (conjunction):
589-
590---   - introduced with `constructor`
591---   - eliminated with `intro ⟨ha, hb⟩` or `obtain ⟨ha, hb⟩ := h`
592-
593--- - `a ∨ b` (disjunction):
594-
595---   - introduced with `left` and `right`
596---   - eliminated with `cases` or `obtain h | h := h`
597-
598--- - `False` (falsehood):
599-
600---   - eliminated with `cases` or `contradiction`
601-
602--- - `¬ a` (negation):
603-
604---   - defined as `a → False`
605-
606--- - `True` (truthhood):
607-
608---   - introduced as `True.intro` or with `constructor`
609-
610--- - `a ↔ b` (iff):
611-
612---   - introduced with `constructor`
613-
614---   - eliminated with `intro ⟨hab, hba⟩`,
615---     `obtain ⟨hab, hba⟩ := h`, or `Iff.mp` and `Iff.mpr`
616-
617--- - `∃ x : α, a` (existential):
618-
619---   - introduced with `exists y`
620---   - eliminated with `intro ⟨x, Hx⟩` or `obtain ⟨x, Hx⟩ := H`
621-
622--- Fundamental connectives we've been using since the
623--- beginning:
624-
625--- - equality (`x = y`)
626--- - implication (`a → b`)
627--- - universal quantification (`∀ x, a`)
628-
629--- ## Programming with Propositions
630-
631--- What does it mean to say that "an element `x` occurs in a
632--- list `l`"?
633-
634--- - If `l` is the empty list, then `x` cannot occur in it, so
635---   the property "`x` appears in `l`" is simply false.
636-
637--- - Otherwise, `l` has the form `[x' :: l']`. In this case, `x`
638---   occurs in `l` if it is equal to `x'` or if it occurs in
639---   `l'`.
640-
641--- We can translate this directly into a straightforward
642--- recursive function taken an element and a list and
643--- returning... a proposition!
644-
645-def List.In {α : Type} (x : α) (xs : List α) : Prop :=
646-  match xs with
647-  | [] => False
648-  | x' :: xs' => x = x' ∨ In x xs'
649-
650-theorem List.In_nil {α : Type} {x : α} : ¬ (List.In x []) := by
651-  dsimp [List.In]; intro h; assumption
652-

679--- ## Applying Theorems to Arguments
680-
681--- Lean also treats *proofs* as first-class objects!
682-
683--- We have seen that we can use `#check` to ask Lean whether an
684--- expression has a given type:
685-
686-#check (Nat.add : Nat → Nat → Nat)
687-
688--- We can also use it to check what theorem a particular
689--- identifier refers to:
690-
691-#check Nat.add_comm
692-
693--- Nat.add_comm (n m : Nat) : n + m = m + n
694-
695-#check Nat.add_assoc
696-
697--- Nat.add_assoc (n m k : Nat) : n + m + k = n + (m + k)
698-
699--- Lean checks the *statements* of the `Nat.add_comm` and
700--- `Nat.add_assoc` theorems in the same way that it checks the
701--- *type* of any term (e.g. `Nat.add`). Leaving off the colon
702--- and the type, Lean prints these types in the infoview for
703--- us.
704-
705--- Why?
706-
707--- The reason is that the identifier `Nat.add_comm` actually
708--- refers to a *proof object* — a logical derivation
709--- establishing the truth of the statement
710--- `∀ n m : Nat, n + m = m + n`. The type of this object is the
711--- proposition that it is a proof of.
712-
713--- The type of an ordinary function tells us what we can do
714--- with it.
715-
716--- - If we have a term of type `Nat → Nat → Nat`, we can give it
717---   two `Nat`s as arguments and get a `Nat` back. Similarly, the
718---   statement of a theorem tells us what we can use that theorem
719---   for.
720-
721--- - If we have a term of type
722---   `∀ n m : Nat, n = m → n + n = m + n`, and we provide it two
723---   numbers `n` and `m` and a third "arugment" of type `n = m`,
724---   we get back a proof object of type `n + n = m + m`.
725-
726--- Lean actually allows us to *apply* a theorem as if it were a
727--- function. This is often handy in proof scripts — e.g.,
728--- suppose we want to prove the following:
729-
730-sf_expect_failure
731-  example (x y z : Nat) : x + (y + z) = (z + y) + x := by
732-    rw [Nat.add_comm]
733-    rw [Nat.add_comm]

737---     they currently leak into `leanOutput` error contexts.
738---     Maybe we should implement a separate scope for declaring
739---     variables only visible to `lean` role instead of `lean`
740---     block.

870--- ## Working with Decidable Properties
871-
872--- We've seen two different ways of expressing logical claims
873--- in Lean: with *booleans* (of type `Bool`), and with
874--- *propositions* (of type `Prop`). Here are the key
875--- differences between `Bool` and `Prop`:
876-
877---   |                     | `Bool` | `Prop` |
878---   | ------------------- | ------ | ------ |
879---   | decidable?          | yes    | no     |
880---   | useable with match? | yes    | no     |
881-
882--- Since functions in Lean by default must terminate on all
883--- inputs, a terminating function of type `Nat → Bool` is a
884--- *decision procedure* — i.e., it yields `true` or `false` on
885--- all inputs.
886-
887--- For example, `Nat.even` is a decision procedure for the
888--- property "is even".
889-
890--- Since `Prop` includes *both* decidable and undecidable
891--- properties, we have two options when we want to formalize a
892--- property that happens to be decidable: we can express it
893--- either as a boolean computation, or as a function into
894--- `Prop`.
895-
896--- For instance, to claim that a number `n` is even, we can say
897--- either that `Nat.even n` evaluates to `true`...
898-
899-example : Nat.even 42 = true := rfl
900-
901--- ... or that there exists some `k` such that `n = double k`.
902-
903-example : Nat.Even 42 := by dsimp [Nat.Even]; exists 21
904-
905--- Of course, it would be deeply strange if these two
906--- characterizations of evenness did not describe the same set
907--- of natural numbers! Fortunately, they do!
908-
909--- To prove this, we first need two helper lemmas.
910-
911-theorem even_double (k : Nat) :
912-    Nat.even (Nat.double k) = true := by
913-  induction k with
914-  | zero => rw [Nat.double_zero]; rfl
915-  | succ k' ih => rw [Nat.double_succ]; exact ih
916-
917--- Note to developers (Yipeng Liu @berberman):
918---     Same issue as `CombineOddEven`.
919-
920-theorem even_double_conv (n : Nat) : ∃ k : Nat,
921-    n = bif Nat.even n then Nat.double k else Nat.double k + 1 := by
922-  sorry
923-
924--- Now the main theorem:
925-
926-theorem Nat.even_bool_prop (n : Nat) : Nat.even n = true ↔ Even n := by
927-  constructor
928-  · intro h
929-    obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ := even_double_conv n
930-    rw [h] at hk; dsimp at hk; dsimp [Even]; exists k
931-  · intro ⟨k, hk⟩; rw [hk]; apply even_double
932-
933--- In view of this theorem, we can say that the boolean
934--- computation `Nat.even n` is *reflected* in the truth of the
935--- proposition `∃ k, n = Nat.double k`.
936-
937--- Similarly, to state that two numbers `n` and `m` are equal,
938--- we can say either
939-
940--- 1. that `n == m` returns `true`, or
941--- 2. that `n = m`.
942-
943--- Again, these two notions are equivalent:
944-
945--- (For the reverse direction we need the simple fact that `==`
946--- is reflexive.)
947-
948-theorem beq_eq_true (n m : Nat) :
949-    (n == m) = true ↔ n = m := by
950-  constructor
951-  · apply beq_eq
952-  · intro h
953-    rw [h]
954-    apply BEq.rfl
955-
956--- So what should we do in situations where some claim could be
957--- formalized as either a proposition or a boolean computation?
958--- Which should we choose?
959-
960--- In general, *both* can be useful. For example, booleans are
961--- more useful for defining functions, since we can test
962--- whether they are true using conditional expressions.
963-
964-def is_even_prime (n : Nat) : Bool :=
965-  bif n == 2 then true else false
966-
967--- The most direct way to prove this is to give the value of
968--- `k` explicitly.
969-
970-example : Nat.Even 100 := by
971-  exists 50
972-
973--- The proof of the corresponding boolean statement is simpler,
974--- because we don't have to invent the witness `50`:
975--- computation does it for us!
976-
977-example : Nat.even 100 := rfl
978-
979--- Now, the useful observation is that, since the two notions
980--- are equivalent, we can use the boolean formulation to prove
981--- the other one without mentioning the value 500 explicitly:
982-
983-example : Nat.Even 100 := by
984-  obtain ⟨h, _⟩ := Nat.even_bool_prop 100
985-  apply h; rfl
986-
987--- Although we haven't gained much in terms of proof-script
988--- simplicity in this case, larger proofs can often be made
989--- considerably simpler by the use of reflection.
990-
991--- As an extreme example, a famous mechanized proof of the even
992--- more famous *four colour theorem* uses reflection ot reduce
993--- the analysis of hundreds of different cases to a boolean
994--- computation.
995-
996--- Another advantage of booleans is that the *negation* of a
997--- claim about booleans is straightforward to state and (when
998--- true) to prove: simply slip the expected boolean result.
999-
1000-example : Nat.even 101 = false := rfl
1001-
1002--- In contrast, propositional negation can be difficult to work
1003--- with directly. For example, suppose we state the nonevenness
1004--- of `101` propositionally:
1005-
1006--- Proving this directly — by assuming that there is some `n`
1007--- such that `101 = Nat.double n` and then somehow reasoning to
1008--- a contradiction — would be rather complicated.
1009-
1010--- But if we convert it to a claim about the boolean `Nat.even`
1011--- function, we can let Lean do the work for us.
1012-
1013-example : ¬ Nat.Even 101 := by
1014-  sorry
1015-
1016--- Conversely, there are situations where it can be easier to
1017--- work with propositions rather than booleans. In particular,
1018--- knowing that `(n == m) = true` is generally of little direct
1019--- help in the middle of a proof involving `n` and `m`. But if
1020--- we convert the statement to the equivalent form `n = m`,
1021--- then we can easily rewrite with it.
1022-
1023-theorem add_beq_true (n m p : Nat) (h : (n == m) = true) :
1024-    (n + p == m + p) = true := by
1025-  sorry

1027--- ## The Logic of Lean
1028-
1029--- Lean's logical core is a "metalanguage for mathematics" in
1030--- the same sense as familiar foundations for paper-and-pencil
1031--- math, like Zermelo–Fraenkel Set Theory (ZFC).
1032-
1033--- Mostly, the differences are not too important, but a few
1034--- points are useful to understand.
1035-
1036--- ### Propositional Extensionality
1037-
1038--- Lean's logic is quite minimalistic. This means that on
1039--- occasionally encounters cases where translating standard
1040--- mathematical reasoning into Lean is cumbersome - or even
1041--- impossible - unless we enrich its core logic with additional
1042--- axioms.
1043-
1044--- A first instance has to do with equality of propositions.
1045-
1046-#check (∀ a b : Prop, (a ∧ b) = (b ∧ a) : Prop)
1047-
1048--- This is an equality between two conjunctions, which itself
1049--- is also a proposition. It states that commuted conjunctions
1050--- are equal propositions. However, we cannot prove this
1051--- equality by reflexivity, as the two sides don't compute to
1052--- the same term, and we cannot proceed by cases on `a` or `b`,
1053--- as they are not inductive.
1054-
1055-sf_expect_failure
1056-  example (a b : Prop) : a ∧ b = b ∧ a := by rfl
1057-
1058--- Tactic `rfl` failed: The left-hand side
1059---   a
1060--- is not definitionally equal to the right-hand side
1061---   b = b ∧ a

1099--- we have seen earlier.

1103--- and_comm {a b : Prop} : a ∧ b ↔ b ∧ a
1104-
1105--- Since it would be convenient to be able to rewrite
1106--- propositions from one side of `↔` to the other, Lean
1107--- provides an axiom to turn `↔` into `=`, which is called
1108--- *propositional extensionality* (`propext`).
1109-
1110-#print propext
1111-
1112--- axiom propext : ∀ {a b : Prop}, (a ↔ b) → a = b
1113-
1114--- Lean provides an `ext` tactic that applies `propext` for us.
1115--- We can use it to show that commuted conjoined propositions
1116--- are equal. Similarly, we can use it to show that
1117--- reassociated conjoined propositions are equal as well.
1118-
1119-theorem and_comm_eq (a b : Prop) : (a ∧ b) = (b ∧ a) := by
1120-  ext; apply and_comm
1121-
1122-theorem and_assoc_eq (a b c : Prop) : ((a ∧ b) ∧ c) = (a ∧ (b ∧ c)) := by
1123-  ext; apply and_assoc
1124-
1125--- Here is an example of where using `=` instead of `↔` is more
1126--- convenient: we show that it's possible to "flip" three
1127--- conjoined propositions.
1128-
1129--- This can be proven by constructing the `↔`, then destructing
1130--- the `↔` in `Nat.add_comm` and `Nat.add_assoc`, then applying
1131--- them a few times. But this is a lot of hassle, when the
1132--- proof is conceptually simple: we flip `b` and `c`, then we
1133--- flip that conjunction with `a`, and we finish by
1134--- associativity. By using `and_comm_eq`, this is easily done
1135--- by rewriting equal propositions.

1137-theorem and_comm_flip (a b c : Prop) : (a ∧ b ∧ c) ↔ (c ∧ b ∧ a) := by

1139-
1140--- The pattern of deriving an equality of propositions out of
1141--- `↔` then rewriting by that equality is so common that Lean
1142--- will implicitly cast `↔` to `=`, allowing you to rewrite on
1143--- `↔` directly. Notice that `rw` is also able to close goals
1144--- of the form `a ↔ a` by reflexivity.

1147-  rw [@and_comm b c, @and_comm a, and_assoc]

1183--- ### Functional Extensionality
1184-
1185--- We can also write propositions claiming that two *functions*
1186--- are equal to each other. In some cases, we can also prove
1187--- that two functions are equal by reflexivity when both reduce
1188--- to the same expression:
1189-
1190-example : (fun x => x + 2) = (fun x => x + (Nat.pred 3)) := rfl
1191-
1192--- In general, functions can be equal for more interesting
1193--- reasons. In common mathematical practice, two functions `f`
1194--- and `g` are considered equal if they produce the same output
1195--- on every input:
1196-
1197---   (∀ x, f x = g x) → f = g
1198-
1199--- This is known as *functional extensionality*, which Lean
1200--- provides as `funext`.
1201-
1202-#check (fun f g => funext (f := f) (g := g) :
1203-    ∀ {α β : Type} (f g : α → β), (∀ x, f x = g x) → f = g)
1204-
1205--- Now we can prove some intuitively obvious equalities about
1206--- functions that would otherwise not be provable without
1207--- `funext`.
1208-
1209-theorem add_comm_fun : (fun (n m : Nat) => n + m) = (fun (n m : Nat) => m + n) := by
1210-  apply funext; intro n
1211-  apply funext; intro m
1212-  exact Nat.add_comm n m
1213-
1214--- The `ext` tactic will also apply `funext` as many times as
1215--- possible, introducing all variables in one go. (The singular
1216--- version of the tactic is `ext1`.)
1217-
1218-theorem add_comm_fun' : (fun (n m : Nat) => n + m) = (fun (n m : Nat) => m + n) := by
1219-  ext n m; exact Nat.add_comm n m

1231--- ### Classical vs. Constructive Logic
1232-
1233--- The following reasoning principle is *not* derivable with
1234--- the tools we've seen so far:
1235-
1236-abbrev excluded_middle := ∀ a : Prop, a ∨ ¬ a
1237-
1238--- Logical systems in which excluded middle does not hold are
1239--- referred to as *constructive logics*. They are so called
1240--- because to prove a proposition, we must give a construction
1241--- for it; for instance, a proof of `∃ x, p x` is proven by
1242--- providing a particular value of `x`.
1243-
1244--- Logical systems in which excluded middle does hold, such as
1245--- ZFC set theory, are referred to as *classical*. Lean
1246--- provides classical reasoning principles in the `Classical`
1247--- library, including excluded middle.
1248-
1249-#check Classical.em
1250-
1251--- Classical.em (p : Prop) : p ∨ ¬p

6--- # Poly: Polymorphism and Higher-Order Functions
7-
8--- ### Polymorphic Lists
9-
10--- Instead of defining new lists for each type, like this...
11-
12-inductive BoolList : Type where
13-  | nil
14-  | cons (b : Bool) (l : BoolList)
15-
16--- ... Lean lets us give a *polymorphic* definition that allows
17--- list elements of any type:
18-
19-inductive MyList (α : Type) : Type where
20-  | nil : MyList α
21-  | cons (x : α) (l : MyList α) : MyList α
22-
23--- We can now write `MyList Nat` in place of a specialized
24--- list-of-numbers type.
25-
26--- What is `MyList` itself?
27-
28--- It is a *type constructor* — a function from types to types.
29-
30--- Note to developers (Yipeng Liu @berberman):
31---     A trick used below: parenthesizing the declaration makes
32---     it a term — Lean elaborates it and prints its inferred
33---     function type, instead of the declaration signature:
34---     `MyList (α : Type) : Type`.
35-
36-#check (MyList)
37-
38--- MyList : Type → Type
39-
40--- The `α` in the definition of `MyList` becomes an implicit
41--- parameter to the list constructors `nil` and `cons`.
42-
43-#check MyList.nil
44-
45--- MyList.nil {α : Type} : MyList α
46-
47-#check MyList.cons 3 MyList.nil
48-
49--- MyList.cons 3 MyList.nil : MyList Nat
50-
51-#check MyList.nil
52-
53--- MyList.nil {α : Type} : MyList α
54-
55-#check MyList.cons
56-
57--- MyList.cons {α : Type} (x : α) (l : MyList α) : MyList α
58-
59--- We can now define polymorphic versions of the functions
60--- we've already seen...
61-
62-def myRepeat (α : Type) (x : α) (count : Nat) : MyList α :=
63-  match count with
64-  | 0 => .nil
65-  | count' + 1 => .cons x (myRepeat α x count')
66-
67--- Some simple facts about `myRepeat`:
68-
69-theorem myRepeat_zero (α : Type) (v : α) : myRepeat α v 0 = MyList.nil := rfl
70-
71-theorem myRepeat_succ (α : Type) (v : α) (count : Nat) :
72-    myRepeat α v (count + 1) = MyList.cons v (myRepeat α v count) := rfl
73-
74-example : myRepeat Nat 4 2 = .cons 4 (.cons 4 .nil) := by rfl
75-
76-example : myRepeat Bool false 1 = .cons false .nil := by rfl
77-
78--- _Quiz:_
79-
80--- What is the type of
81--- `MyList.cons true (MyList.cons 3 MyList.nil)`?
82-
83--- (A) `MyList Nat`
84-
85--- (B) `{α : Type} → α → MyList α → MyList α`
86-
87--- (C) `MyList Bool`
88-
89--- (D) `MyList (Nat × Bool)`
90-
91--- (E) Ill-typed
92-
93--- _Quiz:_
94-
95--- What is the type of `myRepeat`?
96-
97--- (A) `Nat → Nat → MyList Nat`
98-
99--- (B) `(α : Type) → α → Nat → MyList α`
100-
101--- (C) `(α : Type) → {β : Type} → α → Nat → MyList β`
102-
103--- (D) Ill-typed
104-
105--- _Quiz:_
106-
107--- What is the type of `myRepeat 1 2`?
108-
109--- (A) `MyList Nat`
110-
111--- (B) `(α : Type) → α → Nat → MyList α`
112-
113--- (C) `MyList Bool`
114-
115--- (D) Ill-typed
116-
117--- From now on we'll use Lean's built-in `List α` type with
118--- notations `[]`, `::`, `[1, 2, 3]`, and `++`.
119-
120-def list123 : List Nat := [1, 2, 3]
121-
122--- #### Type Annotation Inference
123-
124--- Let's write the definition of `myRepeat` again, but this
125--- time we won't specify the type of the parameter `α`. Will
126--- Lean still accept it?
127-
128-def myRepeat' α (x : α) (count : Nat) : List α :=
129-  match count with
130-  | 0 => .nil
131-  | count' + 1 => .cons x (myRepeat' α x count')
132-
133--- Indeed it will. Lean infers that `α` is a type. The
134--- generated `u_1` is part of Lean's bookkeeping for treating
135--- types more generally. We will not need to interpret names
136--- like this for now — you can ignore them when they appear in
137--- Lean's output unless we explicitly call attention to them.
138-
139-#check myRepeat'
140-
141--- myRepeat'.{u_1} (α : Type u_1) (x : α) (count : Nat) : List α
142-
143--- Lean has used *type inference* to deduce a type for `α`.
144-
145--- #### Type Argument Synthesis
146-
147--- Supplying every type *argument* is also boring, but Lean can
148--- usually infer them:
149-
150-def myRepeat'' (α : Type) (x : α) (count : Nat) : List α :=
151-  match count with
152-  | 0 => []
153-  | count' + 1 => x :: myRepeat'' _ x count'
154-
155--- Alternatively, we can declare arguments implicit by
156--- surrounding them with curly braces instead of parens:
157-
158-def myRepeat''' {α : Type} (x : α) (count : Nat) : List α :=
159-  match count with
160-  | 0 => []
161-  | count' + 1 => x :: myRepeat''' x count'
162-
163--- #### Supplying Type Arguments Explicitly
164-
165--- In general, it's fine to just let Lean infer all type
166--- arguments. But occasionally this can lead to problems:
167-
168--- This fails because Lean can't figure out the type of the
169--- empty list: `def mynil := []` — error: type not known We can
170--- fix this with an explicit type annotation:
171-
172--- We can use the `@` prefix to supply the type argument
173--- explicitly. The `@` makes all implicit arguments of a
174--- function explicit:
175-
176-#check @List.nil
177-
178-def myNil' := @List.nil Nat
179-
180--- @List.nil : {α : Type u_1} → List α
181-

186--- list brackets.)

191-
