1232--- We've seen two different ways of expressing logical claims
1233--- in Lean: with booleans (of type `Bool`), and with
1234--- propositions (of type `Prop`).
1235-
1236--- Here are the key differences between `Bool` and `Prop`:
1237-
1238--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
1239---     Check formatting:
1240-
1241--- - ⠀
1242--- - `Bool`
1243--- - `Prop`
1244--- - decidable?
1245--- - yes
1246--- - no
1247--- - useable with `match`?
1248--- - yes
1249--- - no
1250--- - works with `rewrite` tactic?
1251--- - no
1252--- - yes
1253-
1254--- The crucial difference between the two worlds is
1255--- decidability. Every (closed) Lean expression of type `Bool`
1256--- can be simplified in a finite number of steps to either
1257--- `true` or `false` — i.e., there is a terminating mechanical
1258--- procedure for deciding whether or not it is true.
1259-
1260--- This means that, for example, the type `Nat → Bool` is
1261--- inhabited only by functions that, given a `Nat`, always
1262--- yield either `true` or `false` in finite time; and this, in
1263--- turn, means (by a standard computability argument) that
1264--- there is no function in `Nat → Bool` that checks whether a
1265--- given number is the code of a terminating Turing machine.
1266-
1267--- By contrast, the type `Prop` includes both decidable and
1268--- undecidable mathematical propositions; in particular, the
1269--- type `Nat → Prop` does contain functions representing
1270--- properties like "the nth Turing machine halts." The second
1271--- row in the table follows directly from this essential
1272--- difference. To evaluate a pattern match (or conditional) on
1273--- a boolean, we need to know whether the scrutinee evaluates
1274--- to `true` or `false`; this only works for `Bool`, not
1275--- `Prop`.
1276-
1277--- The third row highlights an important practical difference:
1278--- equality functions like `Nat.beq` that return a boolean
1279--- cannot be used directly to justify rewriting with the
1280--- rewrite tactic; propositional equality is required for this.
1281--- Since `Prop` includes both decidable and undecidable
1282--- properties, we have two options when we want to formalize a
1283--- property that happens to be decidable: we can express it
1284--- either as a boolean computation or as a function into Prop.
1285-
1286--- As an example, we can write
1287-
1288-unseal isEven in
1289-example : isEven 42 := rfl
1290-
1291--- or that there exists some `k` such that `42 = double k`.
1292-
1293-unseal double in
1294-example : Even 42 := by exists 21
1295-
1296--- Of course, it would be deeply strange if these two
1297--- characterizations of evenness did not describe the same set
1298--- of natural numbers!
1299-
1300--- Fortunately, they do! To prove this, we first need two
1301--- helper lemmas.
1302-
1303-theorem even_double (k : Nat) : isEven (double k) = true := by
1304-  induction k with
1305-  | zero =>
1306-    rewrite [double_zero, isEven_zero]
1307-    rfl
1308-  | succ n ih =>
1309-    rewrite [double_succ, isEven_succ_succ]
1310-    exact ih
1311-
1312--- ### Exercise (3 stars): isEven_double_exists ⭐⭐⭐
1313-
1314-theorem isEven_double_exists (n : Nat) :
1315-    ∃ k, n = bif isEven n then double k else double k + 1 := by sorry
1316-
1317--- Now the main theorem:
1318-
1319-theorem isEven_iff_Even {n : Nat} : isEven n = true ↔ Even n where
1320-  mp h := by
1321-    have ⟨k, hk⟩ := isEven_double_exists n
1322-    rewrite [h, cond_true] at hk
1323-    subst hk

19--- Until now, we have been working with our own custom natural
20--- numbers, using the `Nat` type that we defined in
21--- `Basics.lean`.
22-
23--- However, Lean has a built-in type of natural numbers, which
24--- is more powerful and comes with many useful features. They
25--- are very slightly different from our custom `Nat`, but these
26--- differences are mostly superficial. The built-in natural
27--- numbers are defined in the `Init` module, which is
28--- automatically imported by Lean. We will refer to them as
29--- `Nat` as well, but they are not the same as the `Nat` we
30--- defined in `Basics.lean`.
31-
32--- In Lean, programmers and mathematicians don't re-prove the
33--- basic properties of natural numbers from scratch, nor do
34--- they tend to write out `rewrite` steps for basic properties
35--- of natural numbers by hand.

71--- This approach is useful in a textbook for understanding the
72--- structure of natural numbers and for providing early
73--- practice with writing proofs. But it is also tedious in the
74--- long term.
75-

87--- In this chapter we will learn how to use the built-in `Nat`
88--- and some powerful features for computing with and proving
89--- properties about natural numbers. Specifically, we will
90--- learn about `dsimp`, `calc`, and `simp` annotations, which
91--- enable more powerful and concise proofs.
92-
93--- In fact, from now on, we will use the built-in `Nat` type
94--- and its powerful features, writing `Nat.<theorem>` to
95--- reference Lean's version of `<theorem>`.

100--- ### `rfl` and computation with `Nat`
101-
102--- With Lean's `Nat`, much of the computation happens
103--- automatically, and `rfl` suffices to close any equality of
104--- computation on literals.
105-
106-theorem complicated_computation : (2 * 3 + 4 * 5 : Nat) * 6 = 156 := by
107-  rfl
108-
109--- This quickly becomes necessary, as natural numbers quickly
110--- get large!
111-
112--- Of course, `rfl` can't close more complicated goals where
113--- the values of the terms are unknown.
114-
115-theorem rfl_not_enough (n m : Nat) (h : n = m) : n = m := by
116-  -- rfl will not work here!
117-  /- First rewrite the goal with `h`; then the two sides are identical. -/
118-  rewrite [h]
119-  rfl
120-
121--- The same proof can be written more compactly with `rw`. In
122--- this example, `rw [h]` rewrites with `h` and then closes the
123--- resulting reflexive goal.
124-
125-theorem rfl_not_enough' (n m : Nat) (h : n = m) : n = m := by
126-  rw [h]
127-
128--- We will continue to show more powerful tools for
129--- manipulating the context and goal of a proof to bring them
130--- closer to what can be solved with `rfl`.

139-  exact?

165--- ## Structuring proofs with `calc`
166-
167--- In Lean proofs, long `rw` chains are useful, but they are
168--- sometimes hard to read because the intermediate goals are
169--- invisible. Furthermore, sometimes we *know* exactly how we
170--- want to manipulate the terms of a proof, but don't want to
171--- have the tactics like `add_comm` and `add_assoc` "guess"
172--- which subterms to rewrite.
173-
174--- The `calc` tactic writes down the intermediate goals of a
175--- proof, and allows us to specify exactly which rewrite rules
176--- to apply at each step. It is a powerful tool for structuring
177--- proofs, and is often more readable than long `rw` chains.
178-
179--- `calc` is designed to mimic the style of proofs in
180--- mathematics textbooks, which will often look something like
181--- this:
182-
183---   a + (b + c)
184---   = (a + b) + c        ...   [by associativity of addition]
185---   = (b + a) + c        ...   [by commutativity of addition]
186---   = b + (a + c)        ...   [by associativity of addition]
187-
188--- Note how we can see each intermediate step of this proof
189--- when we look at it this way. Let's look at how we might
190--- prove this theorem (i.e., that `a + (b + c) = b + (a + c)`)
191--- in Lean.
192-
193--- First, a proof in the style we already know.
194-
195-theorem add_swap (a b c : Nat) : a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) := by
196-  rw [← Nat.add_assoc, Nat.add_comm a b, Nat.add_assoc]
197-
198--- Here we present the same theorem, written with `calc`. Note
199--- how each intermediate goal is visible in the source.
200-
201-theorem add_swap' (a b c : Nat) : a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) := by
202-  calc a + (b + c) /- one side of the goal is the argument to `calc`... -/
203-    /- ... and each subsequent line is a transformation, with a tactic. -/
204-    a + (b + c) = (a + b) + c := by rw [Nat.add_assoc]
205-    (a + b) + c = (b + a) + c := by rw [Nat.add_comm a b]
206-    /- once a line matches the other side of the equality in the main goal
207-       (in this case `(b + (a + c)`), the calc tactic succeeds. -/
208-    (b + a) + c = b + (a + c) := by rw [Nat.add_assoc]
209-
210--- We can also write the proof like this to be a bit more
211--- concise:
212-
213-theorem add_swap'' (a b c : Nat) : a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) := by
214-  calc a + (b + c)
215-    _ = (a + b) + c := by rw [Nat.add_assoc]
216-    _ = (b + a) + c := by rw [Nat.add_comm a b]
217-    _ = b + (a + c) := by rw [Nat.add_assoc]
218-
219--- Whereas before, the left-hand side of each equality in the
220--- `calc` tactic was repeated from the right-hand side of the
221--- previous one, we can replace the left-hand side entirely
222--- with an `_`. Now our Lean proof looks quite a bit like the
223--- textbook one we saw earlier!
224-

229-  rw [Nat.add_mul, Nat.one_mul, Nat.mul_add, Nat.mul_one, ← Nat.add_assoc]
230-

232--- that you can use `rw?` to find appropriate rules to rewrite
233--- by.
234-
235-theorem succ_mul_succ' (n m : Nat) :
236-    (n + 1) * (m + 1) = n * m + n + m + 1 := by
237-  sorry

240--- particular uses, and both will be tools in your ever-growing
241--- toolbox of tactics.

246--- ## Definitional simplification: `dsimp`
247-
248--- Often, rather than rewriting by a known equation like
249-
250--- `n + succ m = succ (n + m)` using `rw [add_succ]`,
251-
252--- we just want to simplify the function (here `add`)
253--- automatically when we can.
254-
255--- The `dsimp` tactic ("definitionally simplify") unfolds
256--- definitions and performs definitional simplifications. You
257--- can give it hints in square brackets: `dsimp [f]` tells it
258--- to unfold the definition of `f`. You can also simplify a
259--- hypothesis `h` in the context by writing `dsimp [...] at h`.
260--- `dsimp` will also close goals by `rfl` when possible.
261-
262-def square (n : Nat) : Nat := n * n
263-
264-def triple (n : Nat) : Nat := n + n + n
265-
266--- When the goal depends on a fact about an unknown value,
267--- `rfl` fails. Here, `dsimp` makes progress, exposing a goal
268--- the fact can close.
269-
270-example (n m : Nat) (h : n + n = m) : triple n = m + n := by
271-  -- rfl will not work here!
272-  dsimp [triple]
273-  /- The goal can now be rewritten by `h`. -/
274-  rw [h]
275-
276--- As we have seen, `rw` can also unfold definitions. In this
277--- example, either style is fine: use `dsimp [triple]` when you
278--- want to emphasize definitional simplification, or
279--- `rw [triple, h]` when the proof is just a sequence of
280--- rewrites.
281-
282-example (n m : Nat) (h : n + n = m) : triple n = m + n := by
283-  /- `rw [triple]` unfolds `triple n`. -/
284-  rw [triple, h]
285-

287-
288--- Complete this proof, using `dsimp` or `rw` as appropriate.
289-
290-example (n m : Nat) (h : m = n) : triple m = n + (n + n) := by
291-  sorry
292-
293--- `dsimp at h` also works on hypotheses, which rfl can't
294--- touch.
295-
296-example (n : Nat) (h : square n = 16) : n * n = 16 := by
297-  dsimp [square] at h
298-  exact h
299-
300--- Aside: `rw [...] at h` also works on hypotheses too, as does
301--- `rw? at h`
302-
303-example (n m : Nat) (h : 2 * n = m * 2) : n + n = m + m := by
304-  rw [Nat.mul_comm, Nat.mul_two, Nat.mul_two] at h
305-  exact h
306-
307--- `dsimp` also takes definitional steps such as `+ 0`, so it
308--- can finish goals that rfl would close.
309-
310-example (n : Nat) : square n + 0 = n * n := by
311-  dsimp [square]
312-
313--- Like `rw` and `exact`, `dsimp` also has a `?` version that
314--- searches for functions to simplify by. Many Lean tactics
315--- have `?` versions; try it out if you are unsure.

335-  | n + 2 => even n

349-  | 0    => 0
350-  | n' + 1 => double n' + 2

397--- ## Using Code Actions to Generate Match Skeletons
398-
399--- Lean's language server can suggest *code actions*, which are
400--- small editor commands that modify the source code. In
401--- VSCode, a light-bulb icon appears on the left when a code
402--- action is available at your cursor. You can click the icon
403--- or open the code action menu with `Ctrl + .` on
404--- Windows/Linux or `Command + .` on macOS.
405-
406--- For more information, see [Lean 4 VS Code extension
407--- manual](https://github.com/leanprover/vscode-lean4/blob/master/vscode-lean4/manual/manual.md#code-actions).
408-
409--- Some code actions can generate the explicit branches needed
410--- for pattern matching. This is especially useful when working
411--- with `match` expressions, or with tactics such as `cases`
412--- and `induction`, which we saw in previous chapters.
413-
414--- Let's look at an example using `induction`.
